result.summary: Hesiod urges his brother Perses to follow justice rather than violence, describing how Zeus rewards just cities and punishes unjust ones, and how he watches over judges. He then turns to the value of hard work, warning Perses against idleness and the pursuit of other men's property.

scenes.title: Justice beats Outrage
scenes.summary: Hesiod tells Perses to choose justice over violence. Justice is dragged by bribe-eating judges and follows weeping to the city.
scenes.stakes: Perses risks the ruin that comes to those who foster violence and crooked judgement.

scenes.title: Fates of just and unjust cities
scenes.summary: Just cities enjoy peace and plenty, while Zeus punishes cities with famine, plague and defeat for the sins of bad men.
scenes.stakes: Whole cities prosper or perish according to their justice.

scenes.title: Warning to the princes
scenes.summary: Hesiod warns the princes that Zeus's spirits and his daughter Justice watch over crooked judgements. He doubts Zeus will let the unrighteous triumph.
scenes.stakes: Princes who take bribes bring divine punishment on their people.

scenes.title: Right for men, sweat for virtue
scenes.summary: Zeus gave men right, unlike beasts. Honest witnesses prosper, and the path to goodness is steep but eased at the top.
scenes.stakes: Perses could fall into easy badness and lose prosperity and good name.

scenes.title: Work and the idler's shame
scenes.summary: Hesiod tells Perses to work so that Hunger hates him and Demeter loves him. Idleness is disgraceful, and wealth brings renown.
scenes.stakes: Perses risks hunger, poverty and shame if he stays idle and covets others' property.

notable_quotes.reason: A proverb that harm done to others returns upon the doer.
Famous maxim valuing labour over idleness.
Memorable image of virtue as a steep path won by sweat.

analysis.text: Divine justice links the moral order to material prosperity: Zeus rewards honest judgement and punishes crooked rulers.
The passage reflects a farming society where corrupt, bribe-taking local chiefs could decide disputes, as in Hesiod's quarrel with Perses over inheritance.

legacy.text: The image of the steep, rough path to virtue and the easy road to vice influenced later moral writing, including the tale of Heracles' choice.

fun_facts.text: The line numbered 1308 in sentence 33 is a stray footnote marker from the source edition, not part of Hesiod's text.

language_notes.text: "Delusion" translates a Greek idea of ruinous blindness (atē) sent upon men, leading them into harmful acts.
"Go by on the other side" means take the alternate road, the path of justice rather than violence; Justice wins only at the finish of the race.
Oath is personified as a power that follows crooked verdicts: false judgements lead to broken oaths and their punishment.
Justice is "wrapped in mist" so she is unseen as she follows; she brings harm to those who drove her out.
"Reck not" means "pay no heed to"; "reck" is an archaic verb meaning to care about or take account of.
"Thrice ten thousand" means thirty thousand, a large number standing for countless watchers.
"Devour bribes" refers to princes who accept gifts in return for giving judgements in favour of the giver.
Hesiod speaks bitterly: if the unjust win, being righteous is a bad thing. He does not mean it, as the next sentence shows.
"Forswears himself" means swears falsely, breaking or violating an oath.
"Meet" means fitting or suitable; "sluggard" is a lazy person.
The stray number "1308" is a footnote marker from the edition, not part of Hesiod's text.

context_notes.text: Perses is Hesiod's brother, who cheated him of inheritance with bribed judges; the poem is addressed to him.
The "bribe-eating" judges are the local nobles (kings) who settled disputes, here accused of corruption.
Cronos was Zeus's father, the Titan whom Zeus overthrew; "son of Cronos" is a standard title for Zeus.
Justice (Dike) is a goddess, daughter of Zeus. Hesiod presents her as an advocate who reports human wrongdoing to her father.
Perses is Hesiod's brother, who has taken more than his share of the inheritance and gone to law with bribed princes.
Demeter is the goddess of grain and harvest, so her love means a full barn for the farmer.

literary_notes.text: Life's moral choice is a race, with Justice finally overtaking Outrage at the finish.
Justice is imagined as a woman physically dragged through the streets, making the corruption of courts vivid.
Abundant oaks, acorns, bees and fleeces paint a picture of the prosperity that justice brings.
Collective punishment for one man's sin, with famine and plague, shows divine justice as a recurring theme.
The thirty thousand spirits, wrapped in mist, turn the unseen watchfulness of the divine order into a visible crowd of observers.
The sentence is a compact maxim; its balanced halves state that harm done to others returns upon the doer.
The "eye of Zeus" stands for his all-seeing knowledge and judgement.
Badness is pictured as a woman living close by on an easy road, contrasting with the difficult road to Goodness.
Virtue is a steep path that grows easy at the top, showing that hardship at the start is rewarded.
The idle man is compared to drones who eat the bees' labour, making his parasitism vivid.
